_comment: Identification and Authentication Plan generator. Authored at the Phase 2 assessability floor; pairs naturally with the AC plan since AC delegates the underlying identity proofing and authenticator strength to IA.
title: Identification and Authentication Plan
description: Documents how the system identifies users, devices, and services and verifies their authenticators. Covers the controls of the IA family in NIST SP 800-53 r5 and aligns with NIST SP 800-63 (Digital Identity Guidelines) and FIPS 140 (cryptographic modules).
intro_template:
This Identification and Authentication Plan documents the I&A approach for {system_name}. It establishes the practices, technical mechanisms, and credential lifecycle that prove who a user, device, or service is before access decisions in the AC family take effect.

The scope covers identifier management, authenticator management, multi-factor authentication, identity proofing, federation with external identity providers, and re-authentication policies within the {system_name} authorization boundary. The plan is consistent with NIST SP 800-53 r5 (Identification and Authentication family), NIST SP 800-63 (Digital Identity Guidelines), and FIPS 140-3 (Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules) where applicable.
approach_template:
{system_name} authenticates users via {idp_platform} and enforces multi-factor authentication for {mfa_scope}. The system supports {authenticator_types} as authenticator types. Identity proofing is performed at {ial_target} (per NIST SP 800-63A) and authenticator assurance at {aal_target} (per NIST SP 800-63B). Identifier management follows {identifier_strategy}.

Additional details on identifier management, authenticator management, MFA strategy, device authentication, service authentication, non-organizational users, and adaptive / re-authentication are captured in the sub-sections below.
continuous_monitoring_template: Authenticator-related metrics for {system_name} are monitored continuously: failed-authentication rate, authenticator-rotation compliance, expired authenticator counts, and federation outage / lag are reviewed at the cadence in §6.1. Authenticator inventories are reconciled against the authoritative identity store on the cadence below. Continuous-monitoring metrics related to IA controls are documented in the sub-sections below.
integration_template: This Identification and Authentication Plan does not stand alone. The AC family relies on the identities and authenticators established here for its access-control decisions; the AU family records authentication events; and CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring) consumes the authentication-related metrics defined herein. The following cross-references identify the specific artifacts and locations where IA-related content is exchanged with other RMF deliverables.

commonly_inheritable_controls.from: Enterprise federation service (Login.gov / ID.me / SAML federation)

family_questions.label: Approach basics
family_questions.description: Identity provider, supported authenticators, and target assurance levels.

questions.label: Primary identity provider (IdP)
questions.help: The platform that authenticates users and issues identity assertions (e.g., Azure AD / Entra ID, Okta, Ping, Keycloak, AWS IAM Identity Center, ADFS).

questions.label: Scope of MFA enforcement
questions.help: Population required to use MFA. Federal systems handling CUI require AAL2+; privileged often AAL3.

questions.label: Authenticator types supported
options: SMS OTP (deprecated for AAL2+ but documented)
questions.help: Authenticator types supported by this system. NIST SP 800-63B classifies each. Avoid SMS / voice OTP as primary factors at AAL2+.

questions.label: Target Identity Assurance Level (IAL)
questions.help: Per NIST SP 800-63A. Federal systems handling CUI typically require IAL2; classified often IAL3.

questions.label: Target Authenticator Assurance Level (AAL)
questions.help: Per NIST SP 800-63B. Federal CUI typically AAL2; privileged or classified AAL3.

questions.label: Identifier management strategy (one-line)
questions.help: Brief phrase summarizing how identifiers are issued and reused. Detail goes in the dedicated sub-section.

family_questions.label: Identifier Management
family_questions.description: How identifiers are assigned, formatted, reused, and disabled (IA-4).

questions.label: User identifier format
questions.help: Format / convention for usernames (e.g., 'firstname.lastname@org', 'EDIPI for DoD', 'email address from authoritative source').

questions.label: Uniqueness enforcement
questions.help: How identifier collisions are prevented across the user lifecycle, and what disambiguates two people with the same name.

questions.label: Identifier reuse policy
options: Reused only after a defined dormant period (specify)
questions.help: Best practice: never reuse. Federal systems often require minimum 1-2 years of dormancy before reuse, if any.

questions.label: Identifier disable cadence on departure
questions.help: How quickly an identifier is disabled after the user leaves (e.g., '24 hours after HR notification'; 'immediate for involuntary terminations').

questions.label: Device identifier strategy
questions.help: How devices are assigned identifiers (e.g., 'Hostname format <env>-<role>-<n>; X.509 cert with hostname in CN; AD computer object with FQDN matching cert').

questions.label: Service / machine account identifier strategy
questions.help: How service accounts are named (svc- prefix, app-svc-<name>, managed identity, etc.) and how they're distinguished from human users in logs.

family_questions.label: Authenticator Management
family_questions.description: Issuance, distribution, rotation, revocation of authenticators (IA-5).

questions.label: Initial authenticator issuance process
questions.help: How a new user receives their first authenticator. In-person handoff for hardware tokens, signed package for PIV cards, etc.

questions.label: Authenticator distribution method
questions.help: Secure channel used to deliver authenticators (encrypted email with separate password, in-person, registered mail).

questions.label: Rotation / re-issuance cadence
questions.help: By authenticator type (e.g., 'PIV cards every 6 years per FIPS 201; service-account passwords every 60 days; FIDO2 keys lifetime').

questions.label: Revocation workflow
questions.help: How a compromised or surrendered authenticator is revoked across all systems. Time bound (e.g., 'within 4 hours of report').

questions.label: Password / passphrase complexity
questions.help: Length, allowed character classes, breach-list checking, anti-pattern rules. Per NIST SP 800-63B, length matters more than complexity rules.

questions.label: Password storage method
options: Stored only in HSM / hardware credential vault
questions.help: Per NIST SP 800-63B, memorized secrets must be salted and hashed using a memory-hard function.

family_questions.label: Multi-Factor Authentication Strategy
family_questions.description: When MFA is required, methods preferred, and exception handling.

questions.label: MFA scope details
questions.help: Specific scenarios / actions / populations requiring MFA beyond the high-level scope in §4.1.

questions.label: Preferred MFA method
questions.help: Method recommended to users by default. Federal systems should default to hardware-key when feasible (per OMB M-22-09 zero-trust guidance).

questions.label: Phishing-resistance level
questions.help: Per OMB M-22-09, federal systems should adopt phishing-resistant MFA. Document where you stand on the journey.

questions.label: MFA fallback / recovery method
questions.help: What happens when a user loses their primary authenticator. Help-desk verification process, backup codes, or in-person re-issuance.

questions.label: MFA exceptions process
questions.help: Rare scenarios where MFA cannot be enforced (legacy system, embedded service). Time-bound exception register; cross-reference §4.5 of CM Plan if relevant.

family_questions.label: Device Identification and Authentication
family_questions.description: How devices authenticate to the system (IA-3).

questions.label: Device authentication mechanism
questions.help: How devices identify themselves: X.509 client certificates, MDM-issued certs, EAP-TLS, MAC binding (last resort), MFA-bound device identity.

questions.label: Device certificate authority / issuer
questions.help: PKI / CA that issues device certificates (e.g., 'Internal CA on enterprise PKI', 'Microsoft Intune-issued device cert').

questions.label: Device revocation mechanism
questions.help: How a lost / decommissioned device is removed from authentication. CRL / OCSP / cert-bound short-lifetime tokens.

family_questions.label: Service / Machine Authentication
family_questions.description: How services and automated processes authenticate (IA-9).

questions.label: Service authentication mechanism
questions.help: Mechanism: managed identity (cloud-native), workload identity federation, mTLS, signed JWT, API key (last resort), service principal.

questions.label: Service-credential storage / vaulting
questions.help: Where service credentials live (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, CyberArk).

questions.label: Service-credential rotation
questions.help: Cadence + automation for rotating service credentials. Short-lived ephemeral credentials (workload identity) are best practice.

questions.label: Service account ownership model
questions.help: How each service account is assigned to a human owner / role for accountability. Quarterly review against ownership register.

family_questions.label: Non-Organizational Users
family_questions.description: Federation, external partner identities, and public users (IA-8).

questions.label: Federation partners
questions.help: External identity providers federated with the system.

questions.label: IAL/AAL required for external users
questions.help: Assurance levels enforced for non-organizational users — often differ from internal scope.

questions.label: Attribute release policy (federation)
questions.help: Which attributes the external IdP must assert for the user to be authenticated (subject, email, group memberships, MFA satisfied claim).

family_questions.label: Adaptive and Re-authentication
family_questions.description: Risk-based authentication and re-authentication triggers (IA-10, IA-11).

questions.label: Risk signals informing adaptive auth
questions.help: Signals that elevate authentication strength (step-up MFA) when a risk threshold is crossed.

questions.label: Adaptive authentication engine
questions.help: Tool / service evaluating risk signals (e.g., 'Okta Adaptive MFA', 'Azure AD Conditional Access', 'custom risk engine').

questions.label: Maximum session duration before forced re-auth
questions.help: Hard cap on session length before user must re-authenticate (per AAL2: 12h interactive / 30 days non-interactive; per AAL3: 12h / 18h).

family_questions.label: Identity Populations Supported
family_questions.description: Numerical scope of who authenticates to this system.

family_questions.label: Authentication Metrics & KPIs
family_questions.description: Metrics tracked to demonstrate IA control effectiveness over time.

family_questions.label: Cross-references to other RMF artifacts
family_questions.description: Where this plan plugs into the broader RMF package.

questions.label: SSP section reference
questions.help: Where in the SSP the IA control implementations are summarized (e.g., 'SSP §13.4').

questions.label: POA&M ID prefix for IA findings
questions.help: Convention for IA-related POA&M items (e.g., 'POAM-IA-').

questions.label: AC plan cross-reference
questions.help: Where the AC plan consumes IA outputs. AC delegates the underlying authenticator strength and identity proofing to IA.

questions.label: AU event handoff
questions.help: How authentication events (success / failure / step-up) flow into the AU pipeline. SIEM index, log source, retention.

questions.label: CA-7 continuous-monitoring strategy reference
questions.help: Pointer to the CA-7 monitoring strategy document tying IA continuous-monitoring metrics to the broader ConMon plan.

prompts: Reference §4.1 — IdP platform, MFA scope, AAL target.
State the MFA enforcement mechanism and what populations it covers.
Address phishing-resistant MFA per OMB M-22-09 — see §4.4.
Document the AAL achieved per population (privileged often AAL3, standard AAL2).
Reference IA-2(1) MFA for privileged accounts, IA-2(2) MFA for non-privileged, IA-2(8) replay-resistant, IA-2(12) PIV credentials acceptance.
evidence_suggestions: Sample authentication audit log showing MFA success

extra_fields.label: AAL achieved per user population
extra_fields.help: Map each user type to its actual AAL (e.g., 'Privileged: AAL3 hardware key only; Standard internal: AAL2 push or TOTP; External federated: AAL2 via partner attestation').

extra_fields.label: Phishing-resistant MFA status
extra_fields.help: Where the system is on the OMB M-22-09 journey: full coverage, partial, planned. Link to the implementation roadmap if applicable.

prompts: Identify the device authentication mechanism — see §4.5.
Describe the device certificate or token issuance authority.
Document how device identity is bound to user identity for combined access decisions.
Address device authentication for IoT / OT / embedded devices if any.
Reference IA-3(1) cryptographic bidirectional authentication, IA-3(4) device attestation.
Describe the identifier format and uniqueness enforcement — see §4.2.
Document the identifier reuse policy and disable cadence.
Address identifier issuance for service / machine accounts.
Reference IA-4(4) identify status of individuals (e.g., contractor vs employee marker).

extra_fields.label: User-status identification method
extra_fields.help: How the system distinguishes employees, contractors, vendors, partners in their identifiers (prefix / suffix / attribute / OU). References IA-4(4).

prompts: Reference §4.3 — issuance, rotation, revocation processes.
Document password complexity, storage method, and breach-list checking — see §4.3.
Address authenticator-strength requirements per type.
Describe initial-authenticator-content protection (sealed envelope, MFA-protected reveal).
Reference IA-5(1) password-based, IA-5(2) public-key based, IA-5(6) authenticator protection, IA-5(7) no embedded unencrypted authenticators.

extra_fields.label: Breach-list checking for passwords
options: Yes — checked against curated breach corpus on every set / change
extra_fields.help: Per NIST SP 800-63B, memorized secrets should be screened against breached corpora.

extra_fields.label: Verification that no unencrypted authenticators are embedded in code / config
extra_fields.help: How the org verifies IA-5(7) — secret scanning in CI, pre-commit hooks, periodic codebase scan, attestation.

prompts: Identify the cryptographic modules used for authentication.
State the FIPS 140-2 or 140-3 validation level (140-2 Level 1/2/3/4 or 140-3 equivalent).
Reference the CMVP certificate number for each module.
Address how non-validated modules are prevented from being used in authentication paths.
evidence_suggestions: FIPS 140 module inventory with CMVP cert numbers
Cryptographic-module configuration showing FIPS mode enabled

extra_fields.label: FIPS 140-validated modules in use
extra_fields.help: Each module + its CMVP certificate number (e.g., 'OpenSSL FIPS Provider cert #4282; Microsoft CNG cert #4536').

extra_fields.label: FIPS 140 version targeted
options: FIPS 140-2 (legacy; 140-2 modules accepted through their sunset)
extra_fields.help: FIPS 140-2 is sunsetting; new validations are FIPS 140-3. Document which version each module holds.

prompts: Reference §4.7 — federation partners and IAL/AAL for external users.
Describe the trust establishment with each federation partner.
Document the attribute release policy for incoming federated assertions.
Address de-provisioning when a federation partner removes a user.
Reference IA-8(1) PIV credentials accepted, IA-8(2) approved IdP services, IA-8(4) discovery / federation services.

extra_fields.label: Per-partner IAL/AAL accepted
extra_fields.help: Map each federation partner to the highest IAL / AAL the system accepts from them. Some partners may only assert IAL1; constrain access accordingly.

extra_fields.label: Attribute validation on inbound assertion
extra_fields.help: How asserted attributes are validated (signature verification, attribute-source whitelist, freshness checks).

prompts: Document re-authentication triggers — see §4.8.
State the maximum session duration before forced re-auth (per AAL).
Address re-authentication for privilege elevation, sensitive operations, and risk events.
Document any user-friendly mechanisms (silent re-auth where possible vs intrusive).
Reference IA-11 ODV: organization-defined circumstances or situations.
evidence_suggestions: Sample audit log showing forced re-auth event

extra_fields.label: Session duration per role
extra_fields.help: Map roles to their max session length and re-auth interval (e.g., 'Privileged: 4h interactive; Standard: 8h; Public users: per-request stateless').

prompts: Reference §4.1 IAL target.
Describe the identity-proofing process used.
Document evidence collected and retained per IAL — see NIST SP 800-63A Table 5-1 / 5-2.
Address remote vs in-person proofing pathways.
Reference IA-12(1) supervisor authorization, IA-12(2) identity evidence, IA-12(3) identity evidence validation, IA-12(4) in-person validation, IA-12(5) address confirmation.

extra_fields.label: Proofing method
options: Remote with verifiable evidence (NIST SP 800-63A IAL2)
Inherited from federation partner (Login.gov / ID.me / CAC)

extra_fields.label: Evidence retention period
extra_fields.help: How long identity-proofing evidence is retained (per NIST SP 800-63A and organizational records-retention policy).

glossary.definition: Verifying that a claimed identity is the actual identity of the entity making the claim, typically by demonstrating control over an authenticator.
A means used to confirm an identity, such as a password, hardware token, biometric, or cryptographic key.
Per NIST SP 800-63B, a measure of the strength of authentication: AAL1 single-factor, AAL2 multi-factor, AAL3 hardware-bound multi-factor verifier-impersonation-resistant.
Authentication based on physiological or behavioral characteristics, typically used as one factor with a hardware-bound key.
An entity that issues digital certificates binding identifiers to public keys. Note: shares acronym with the CA control family.
Hardware or software that implements cryptographic operations. FIPS 140 governs module validation for federal use.
An arrangement where identity assertions issued by one trust domain are accepted by another, typically via SAML or OIDC.
An open standard for phishing-resistant MFA using hardware-bound public-key cryptography. Recommended for high-assurance scenarios.
Federal Information Processing Standard for cryptographic modules. FIPS 140-2 is sunsetting; FIPS 140-3 is current.
A unique label assigned to a user, device, or service to distinguish it from others within a system.
Per NIST SP 800-63A, a measure of how rigorously a real-world identity is bound to a digital account: IAL1 self-asserted, IAL2 verified evidence, IAL3 in-person with biometric.
The process of collecting and verifying evidence that a person is who they claim to be, performed before issuing a credential.
Authentication using questions only the legitimate user should be able to answer. Considered weak by current NIST guidance.
Authentication using at least two factors from distinct categories (something you know, have, or are).
Assurance that the originator of an action cannot later deny performing it. Achieved via digital signatures and tamper-evident audit.
A single-use password, typically generated by an authenticator app (TOTP / HOTP) or hardware token.
Personal Identity Verification (federal civilian) / Common Access Card (DoD) — hardware tokens carrying X.509 certificates for authentication.
MFA that cannot be defeated by an attacker who tricks the user into entering credentials on a fake site. FIDO2 / WebAuthn and PIV / CAC are phishing-resistant.
The system of CAs, certificates, revocation lists, and procedures that issues and manages certificates binding identities to keys.
Repeating the authentication process after the initial sign-in, typically triggered by elevated risk, sensitive operations, or session aging.
Property of an authentication exchange that prevents an attacker who captures the exchange from replaying it later. Required for AAL2+.
An account used by automation, applications, or services rather than humans. Subject to additional rotation, isolation, and ownership requirements.
An active authenticated interaction between a user (or process) and the system. Bounded by sign-in and sign-out / timeout.
Time-based / HMAC-based One-Time Password algorithms (RFC 6238 / RFC 4226), typically delivered via authenticator apps.
Property of an authenticator that prevents a man-in-the-middle from impersonating the verifier and capturing the authentication. Required for AAL3.
Access model that does not implicitly trust any subject or device based on network location and continuously evaluates trust at each access decision.
